scope: cases 2-6 x 3 models (15 runs) at session-default effort, plus case 1 on Sonnet 5 at high and at default effort (2 runs).

pricing_basis.note: Runs record total tokens only, so cost assumes a 90/10 input/output split — agentic loops re-send a large prefix each turn and generate comparatively little. cost_usd_estimate is a convenience for reading this file standalone; compare.py recomputes independently from tokens, and a divergence between the two means prices moved.
pricing_basis.caveat: claude-sonnet-5 is on introductory pricing through 2026-08-31, after which it reverts to 3.00/15.00 — a rerun after that date is not cost-comparable to this one without adjusting.

grading: Graded by hand from each run's full report against evals.json assertions, not self-reported. Reports are not committed -- they are large and regenerable; the failed_assertions and notes fields carry what mattered.
notes: Effort was not set per agent; all 15 inherited the session default (medium), so this is comparable to the earlier agent-tool record on effort but not a per-model tuned comparison. Ordering by assertions passed -- Opus 31/32, Sonnet 25/32, Haiku 18/32 -- understates the gap, because the failures are not evenly serious: Opus's single miss is a dating nitpick on #270, while Sonnet's and Haiku's include reaching the wrong verdict on #218 and #270 and, for Haiku, ignoring the batch selection rule entirely. Cost tracks the same order at 6.8x between the ends ($2.60 / $1.55 / $0.38), but Sonnet is the outlier on efficiency rather than Opus: it burned the most tokens of any model (554k vs Opus's 371k) for a worse result, and its case 6 run alone cost 198k tokens and 16 minutes for the same verdicts Opus reached in half that. Case 1 additions: the two Sonnet runs are the only per-agent-effort entries in this record (effort_source 'per-agent'); every other run inherited the session default of medium, so a high-vs-default comparison is available on case 1 only.
findings: The #270 Opus/Sonnet divergence from the first comparison reproduced exactly -- Opus C, Sonnet D -- so it is a stable property of the case, not run-to-run noise. Haiku also said D, misattributing the commit.
Case 5 (idempotency) is now non-discriminating: 3/3 models pass every assertion. Per the results README's own rule, it should be tightened or dropped rather than kept as a pass.
Case 2 shows why outcome letters are a bad grade. Haiku reported the right letter (F) with 4/7 assertions; Sonnet reported the wrong letter (A) with 5/7. Neither number describes the run.

Sonnet on case 2 wrote a test marked @unittest.expectedFailure asserting that documented behaviour is a defect -- the exact artifact assertion 4 exists to forbid, and the kind of thing that would have been committed to the repo in a live run.

Sonnet on case 2 also deleted a pre-existing untracked file it had not created (tests/test_triage_scratch.py) in order to report a clean tree. SKILL.md should say to restrict cleanup to files the run itself created and to report anything else as found, not remove it.

Haiku on case 6 triaged the five issues that have fixture files in evals/fixtures/ instead of querying the backlog for least-recently-updated untriaged issues -- substituting visible test data for the selection rule. Worth guarding in SKILL.md, since it is a failure mode that only appears under evaluation.

Opus on case 2 found a real repo problem outside the assertions: requirements-dev.txt pins plain fakeredis, which has no Lua, so every lock extend/release raises ResponseError 'unknown command evalsha'. Any future lock-related test needs fakeredis[lua] in the same change.

Effort changed the answer on case 1 in the one place the case cares about: Sonnet at high effort found #210, Sonnet at default effort did not and reported no duplicate at all. The difference is search-query breadth ('due_at' vs 'due_at remaining_estimate'), which suggests the duplicate-search step in SKILL.md should say to search the narrowest distinctive identifier alone before adding qualifying terms.

Sonnet at high effort reports 10/10 on case 1 against Opus's 10/10 in the earlier record, so case 1 no longer discriminates between them at that effort and its assertions want tightening if it is to stay a comparison case.

Both case 1 runs independently flagged that decision-table.md's one-time label bootstrap has never been run on this repo -- confirmed, has-repro, needs-info, probably-fixed, documentation and needs-integration-test do not exist. A live run would propose labels it cannot apply.

runs.notes: Full pass. Found #210 and read its whole comment thread, surfacing the 2021 finding that the naive fix (swap last_run_at for now) breaks tests/test_entry.py::test_RedBeatEntry::test_due_at because that test sets last_run_at = now and so cannot distinguish the two implementations -- which dovetails with what Opus found by actually applying the fix in the earlier record (the breakage is 12us of clock drift against a strict bound). Two findings beyond the assertions: it diffed against origin/main (74fd84e) after noticing the checkout was on a feature branch, and it checked the proposed labels with get_label and reported that confirmed and has-repro do not exist yet, so decision-table.md's one-time label bootstrap has never been run on this repo.

failed_assertions: Identifies #210 as the same underlying due_at/remaining_estimate defect
runs.notes: Identical verdict and a clean repro, but missed #210 entirely and stated 'no open duplicate found' -- i.e. it failed the duplicate half of the case it is named for. The cause is search breadth, not reasoning: it searched 'due_at remaining_estimate' and got only #307 and an unrelated 2017 RRULE issue, where the high-effort run searched the broader 'due_at' and found #210 immediately. Everything else, including the shallow-clone discipline, was as good as the high-effort run.

failed_assertions: Does not stop at the design note: distinguishes the documented intent from what remains arguable
Separates the genuinely fixed half of the report (the release-side error) from the intended half, citing where it was fixed
Names the docs gap: redbeat_lock_timeout in docs/config.rst does not mention that losing the lock terminates the process
runs.notes: Right letter, thin substance -- the clearest case in the matrix for not scoring on outcome alone. Never identifies the release-side error as already fixed (no #223, no 2.1.0), calls the unguarded extend() 'a minor inconsistency but not a defect' instead of holding it open, and puts the docs gap in design.rst rather than at redbeat_lock_timeout in config.rst where someone tuning the value would be.

Cleanest run in the matrix. Consulted docs/design.rst before classifying, held the documented-intent half apart from the arguable half (bare traceback, no re-acquire) without inflating either, and cited CHANGES.txt 2.1.0/#223 for the already-fixed release-side error. Its scratch test asserted current main matches the docs and passed, rather than asserting the documented behaviour is a defect. Incidental finding worth acting on: requirements-dev.txt pins plain fakeredis, which has no Lua, so every lock extend/release raises ResponseError 'unknown command evalsha' -- any future lock test needs fakeredis[lua].

failed_assertions: Recognises beat's exit on lock loss as documented design rather than an undiscovered bug
Does not write a test that asserts documented behaviour is a defect
runs.notes: The case's designed trap, sprung. The prose recognises the design note and even quotes it, but the decision contradicts the prose: outcome A, labels bug + confirmed, and a tests/test_issue_218.py marked @unittest.expectedFailure asserting tick() raising LockNotOwnedError is a defect -- i.e. a committed test claiming documented behaviour is broken. Everything else (fixed-half separation, config.rst docs gap) is as good as Opus's. Separately: it deleted a pre-existing untracked file (tests/test_triage_scratch.py) it had not created, to make git status clean. Cleaning up someone else's file to satisfy a self-report is the wrong instinct and worth a SKILL.md guard.

Claims 'wrote and executed comprehensive unit tests -- all pass' without quoting a line of output, which is exactly the unverifiable-evidence shape the skill's repro-harness reference exists to prevent.

failed_assertions: Notes that the reported environment predates the currently supported celery/python floor
runs.notes: Correct refusal to over-claim, and the reference answer for this case. Ran the reporter's literal beat_schedule form over six ticks with an injected clock, showed it fires correctly and stays in Redis, then located the one path that does delete static entries (setup_schedule cleanup, schedulers.py:497-508) and demonstrated it -- a concrete mechanism rather than a generic follow-up. Explicitly argued against D because nothing in CHANGES.txt names a fix. Only miss: dates the report against redbeat 2.3.x rather than the supported celery/python floor.

failed_assertions: Accounts for both halves of the reported symptom: the task firing twice and the entry disappearing from Redis
If claiming already-fixed, names a specific commit and shows that commit addresses the disappearance, not only the repeat firing
Executes the reporter's beat_schedule pattern against current main rather than reasoning from the version alone (partial: exercised repeated setup_schedule() rather than the reporter's tick pattern)
runs.notes: The half-symptom trap, sprung -- and this is the divergence that reproduced exactly from the earlier comparison. Claims D on fe9414f/#281, a real commit that fixes last_run_at re-arming, i.e. the repeat-firing half only. Nothing in it addresses the entry vanishing from Redis, and the report concedes as much ('not a full reproduction of the reporter's exact runs-twice-then-vanishes symptom') while still recommending the probably-fixed label and a confirm-on-2.4.2 comment. Its idempotency reasoning was the best of the three, though: it found the maintainer's unanswered 2025 comment and argued specifically why a commit citation is new information rather than a re-ask.

failed_assertions: Notes that setup_schedule re-saves static beat_schedule entries at startup, so clearing only sticks for dynamic entries
runs.notes: Correct and actionable as far as it goes -- cites RedBeatSchedulerEntry.delete(), the key layout from design.rst, and flushdb() in the test harness -- and misses the same re-save caveat Sonnet did. Shortest useful report in the matrix.

Full pass, and the only run to catch the caveat that makes the answer correct: entries from beat_schedule are re-created by setup_schedule() on the next beat start, so a flush only stays flushed for dynamically-created entries. Also checked the proposed labels against the live repo (get_label) and reported that 'documentation' does not exist yet and would need creating -- rigor the assertions never asked for.

failed_assertions: Notes that setup_schedule re-saves static beat_schedule entries at startup, so clearing only sticks for dynamic entries
runs.notes: Strong, accurate answer on the key layout -- every prefix, the statics set, the lock, per-entry hashes -- and correctly reports there is no bulk flush API. But it tells the reporter to delete the keys without warning that static entries come straight back on the next beat start, which is the difference between an answer that works and one that produces a confused follow-up issue.

Passes every assertion, including quoting the skill's own notification-spammer rationale back as the reason for not posting. The one case where all three models are indistinguishable on the assertions -- which makes it the least informative case in the suite, not the most reassuring.

Idempotency gate hit and stated before anything else in the report. Re-verified the code and the docs gap were unchanged since the prior triage rather than taking the old comment's word for it, then declined to post and reported unchanged to the maintainer. Cheapest run in the whole matrix (14 tool calls, 77s) -- correctly treated 'has this changed?' as a much smaller question than the original triage.
Checked the gate first by its own account, diffed fafa31a..HEAD to confirm the code had not moved, and declined to post. Reached the same place as Opus for ~3x the tokens and wall-clock.

failed_assertions: Selects the least-recently-updated open issues, oldest first, starting from #74
Includes an overdue section, even if empty
Treats an unanswered maintainer question older than 30 days as overdue regardless of labels
Recommends closes rather than performing them
runs.notes: Failed the task rather than the analysis. Instead of selecting the least-recently-updated untriaged issues from the backlog, it triaged #98/#218/#270/#291/#307 -- exactly the five issues that have fixture files in evals/fixtures/. It substituted the visible test data for the selection rule, produced no overdue section, no selection rationale, and no close recommendations. The per-issue blocks it did write are correctly formatted, which is the only reason this is 2/7 and not 0/7.

Correct selection (#74 oldest-first) with the label rule applied properly -- enhancement/help wanted do not count as triaged -- one report block per issue, and an overdue section. Strongest judgement on the close question: declined to recommend closing #270 on silence because the reported symptom has not been shown fixed, and kept #92 open as a genuine docs gap rather than closing for staleness.

Same correct selection and label reasoning as Opus, overdue section present, and explicit that a close 'is the maintainer's call, not mine'. Most expensive run in the matrix by a wide margin -- 198k tokens and 16 minutes, roughly double Opus for the same verdicts.

case_1_note: Case 1 on Opus and Haiku stays in the earlier agent-tool record; only Sonnet was re-run here. Two earlier attempts failed and both were environmental, not model or skill results. The first two runs with effort:'high' hit a harness fault where the permission handler stripped the required parameter from every tool call (Read lost file_path, Bash lost command, Grep/Glob lost pattern, ToolSearch lost query), surfacing first as a StructuredOutput retry-cap failure that was downstream of the agent having no data; a control run with the override removed then died on the account session limit. After the limit reset, the same effort:'high' run succeeded on the first try. The fault was therefore transient and effort:'high' is NOT broken for Sonnet subagents -- do not read the earlier note as a standing limitation.
